title: Scoping MCP Tools and Guardrails for a Supply Agent
description: Amberlyn Robotics connects a custom agent to an internal inventory system via MCP and must decide how to scope its tools and permissions. The scenario tests recognizing MCP server configuration shapes, applying least-privilege tool scoping, and distinguishing reversible from irreversible actions when designing guardrails.

scenario.background: Amberlyn Robotics builds warehouse automation hardware. Its platform team is standing up a custom agent, "supply-bot," that should check stock levels, flag low-inventory parts, and open restock pull requests against a supplier-config repo. supply-bot needs to talk to the company's internal inventory API and to GitHub. Two engineers are configuring the integration before it goes live.

characters.name: Elena Vasquez
characters.concern: Wiring supply-bot's MCP server connections correctly and scoping its tool grants to exactly what the restock workflow requires.

characters.name: Tomas Reyes
characters.concern: Making sure supply-bot cannot take irreversible inventory or procurement actions without explicit human sign-off, and that its credentials follow least privilege.

questions.stem: Elena configures the inventory system's integration with: `{"type": "remote", "url": "https://inventory.amberlyn.internal/mcp", "auth": {"type": "oauth"}}`. What does this configuration represent?
options: A: A local, stdio-based MCP server that supply-bot's environment launches as a subprocess
B: A remote MCP server reached over HTTPS using OAuth-based authentication, rather than a subprocess launched by supply-bot's environment
C: A GitHub Actions workflow step that runs before supply-bot's session begins
D: A custom agent definition file specifying frontmatter tools
questions.explanation: B is correct because the presence of a `url` and an `auth` block is exactly how a remote MCP server is identified — supply-bot reaches it over the network rather than spawning it locally. A is wrong because a local/stdio server is identified by `command`/`args` fields to launch a subprocess, which are absent here. C and D misidentify the JSON shape entirely — there is no workflow/job structure (C) and no YAML frontmatter with tools (D); this is specifically an MCP server connection descriptor.

questions.stem: Tomas requires that supply-bot can check stock levels and flag low-inventory parts, but must never directly delete or zero-out an inventory record, under any circumstance. What is the most reliable way to enforce this?
options: A: Add an instruction to supply-bot's system prompt telling it never to delete inventory records
B: Grant supply-bot the inventory MCP server's read and update-quantity tools only, excluding the delete-record tool from its configuration entirely
C: Grant full inventory API access and rely on the inventory system's own audit log to catch any deletions after the fact
D: Run supply-bot with an inventory-admin service account, since admin accounts include built-in confirmation prompts for destructive actions
questions.explanation: B is correct because a constraint that must hold under every circumstance needs to be enforced at the capability layer — if the delete tool is never in supply-bot's configuration, there is no code path by which it can be invoked, regardless of how the agent reasons about a given task. A is a soft instruction the model could deviate from under ambiguous or manipulated input. C grants the exact capability compliance wants withheld and only detects misuse after it already happened. D assumes a behavioral safeguard that broad admin credentials do not reliably provide, and grants more capability than the task requires.

questions.stem: supply-bot is allowed to fully autonomously open a restock pull request when stock for a part drops below a threshold — a reversible, easily-reviewed action. Tomas is deciding the autonomy level for a second capability: autonomously cancelling an in-flight purchase order with a supplier once placed. How should this second capability be classified?
options: A: The same autonomy level as opening a restock PR, since both are just inventory-related actions

B: A higher-risk action requiring human approval before execution, since cancelling a placed purchase order may be difficult or costly to reverse and has direct financial and supplier-relationship consequences
C: A lower-risk action than opening a restock PR, since cancelling an order reduces spend rather than committing to it
D: Fully autonomous, as long as the cancellation is logged for later audit
questions.explanation: B is correct because autonomy tiers should track blast radius and reversibility, not surface similarity — opening a PR is reviewable and cheaply undone, while cancelling a live purchase order has real-world financial and supplier consequences that may not be reversible at all. A and C both conflate "inventory-related" with "similar risk," ignoring that the two actions have very different consequences if wrong. D substitutes after-the-fact logging for the approval gate the action actually needs — an audit trail explains what happened, it doesn't prevent the irreversible action from happening.

questions.stem: A developer requests that supply-bot's GitHub App installation be granted org-wide `repo` scope "just in case it needs to touch another repository later," even though its current restock workflow only ever opens PRs against the single supplier-config repo. What should Elena and Tomas do?
options: A: Grant the org-wide scope now to avoid a reconfiguration request later
B: Scope the installation to only the supplier-config repository that the current workflow actually uses, and expand it later if a concrete new task requires it
C: Grant org-wide scope but restrict it to read-only, since read access is always considered safe regardless of scope
D: Deny GitHub access entirely until every future repository supply-bot might ever touch is identified in advance
questions.explanation: B is correct and reflects least privilege: grant exactly what the current, concrete task requires, and expand only when a real task demonstrably needs it — not preemptively for a hypothetical future. A is capability creep justified by convenience, the same anti-pattern Tomas is trying to avoid in the inventory system. C is wrong because org-wide read scope still exposes far more repositories than the task requires, and "read is always safe" ignores that broad read access itself can leak sensitive data across repos supply-bot has no legitimate reason to see. D is impractical and unnecessary — least privilege means scoping to current needs, not requiring omniscient upfront planning.

keyLearnings: MCP server configurations with `command`/`args` describe a local, stdio-launched subprocess; configurations with `url` and an `auth` block describe a remote, network-reached server — recognizing the shape tells you which one you're looking at.
A hard compliance constraint ("never do X") is enforced reliably by excluding the tool that does X from the agent's configuration, not by instructing the agent not to use it.
Autonomy level should be assigned based on an action's blast radius and reversibility, not its surface similarity to other actions the agent already performs.

Least privilege applies to credentials and app installation scopes exactly as much as to individual tool grants — scope to what the current task needs, and expand only when a concrete new task requires it.
